Domain Boundaries & Primary Tools/Methods 
Knowledge Domain Boundaries: This body of literature defines an interdisciplinary knowledge domain focused 
on sustainable, energy-efficient, and real-time intelligent production planning and scheduling (PPS) within 
heavy, energy-intensive process industries—specifically iron and steel manufacturing, heat treatment 
facilities, forging operations, and advanced job-shop systems[1]. Its boundaries encompass the entire production 
chain: from raw ironmaking-steelmaking interfaces and ladle dispatching[26][36], through gas-fired and electric 
reheating furnaces[1], to continuous/intermittent rolling mills[58][59] and Industry 5.0 human-in-the-loop shop-floor 
operations[33][51]. 
Primary Tools and Methods Identified: 
1. Mathematical Programming & Metaheuristics: Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP), Benders' 
decomposition, and chance-constrained/robust optimization (RO) handle rigorous constraints and 
uncertainties[18]. Evolutionary and swarm metaheuristics—such as NSGA-II, Multi-Objective Particle 
Swarm Optimization (MOPSO), Grey Wolf Optimizer (GWO), and Multi-Objective Variable Neighborhood 
Search (MOVNS)—are extensively applied to discover Pareto-optimal trade-offs between energy 
consumption, tardiness, and makespan[2]. 
2. Artificial Intelligence & Reinforcement Learning: Machine learning surrogate models (Support Vector 
Regression, LightGBM, and Genetic Algorithm-BP Neural Networks) predict physical parameters like 
energy consumption and rolling forces[2]. Advanced Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) algorithms—
including Soft Actor-Critic (SAC), Deep Q-Networks (DQN), and Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning 
(MARL) with attention mechanisms or Large Language Model (LLM) reward shaping—enable sub-second 
real-time dynamic rescheduling under spot market electricity tariffs and renewable energy 
fluctuations[5]. 
3. Cyber-Physical Systems & Trustworthy Explainable AI (XAI): Digital Twins built on Asset 
Administration Shells (AAS) and IoT frameworks provide real-time virtual-physical synchronization[6]. To 

overcome black-box opacity and foster human operator trust, explainable AI techniques—such as 
multi-objective counterfactual explanations, decision trees, feature-attribution saliency maps, and 
Intelligence Augmentation (IA) safety layers—ensure transparent, human-centric industrial control.

Analysis of Knowledge Clusters & Structural Relationships 
1. Knowledge Concentrations (Dominant Clusters) 

• Cluster 1 & 2 Core (Thermal Mechanics + Mathematical Metaheuristics): The largest concentration of 
literature focuses on optimizing reheating furnaces, heat treatment lines, and rolling sequences using 
mathematical models (MILP , Benders' decomposition)[1][2] and population-based algorithms (NSGA-II, 
MOPSO, GWO)[3]. These methods resolve physical operational trade-offs between thermal holding 
energy, slab residence times, and product delivery schedules[6][7]. 
• Cluster 3 & 4 Nexus (Cyber-Physical Systems + Autonomous DRL): A rapidly expanding body of 
research connects Industrial IoT platforms and Digital Twins (AAS, 5D walking beam models)[8][9] to Deep 
Reinforcement Learning agents (MAPPO, DSAC)[10][11]. These systems dynamically adapt production 
schedules to volatile electricity spot-market pricing and intermittent renewable energy generation 
without manual intervention[12][11]. 
2. Isolated & Peripheral Domain Nodes 
• Process Safety 4.0 & Intelligence Augmentation ( Process safety 4.0...pdf ): This source is relatively 
isolated from the core algorithmic scheduling papers. While most of the corpus focuses on autonomous 
throughput and energy optimization, this work examines chemical process safety hazards, arguing that 
fully autonomous AI presents grave operational risks during unexpected disruptions[13]. It advocates for 
Intelligence Augmentation (IA)—keeping humans in the decision loop—creating a structural boundary 
between raw efficiency optimization and industrial safety compliance[13]. 
• Fuzzy Uncertainty in Gas Processing ( Batch scheduling...pdf ): While uncertainty is frequently 
modeled using stochastic dynamic programming or DRL, fuzzy numbers for natural gas heating values 
and due dates represent a specialized, less connected niche compared to mainstream DRL and 
metaheuristic approaches[14][15]. 
3. Hidden Structural Relationships & Methodological Bridges 
• NSGA-II as the Bridge Between Optimization and Counterfactual XAI: A crucial structural link exists 
between population-based metaheuristics and Explainable AI [5]. Rather than using NSGA-II purely to 
minimize production makespan, modern frameworks deploy it to perform multi-objective searches for 
counterfactual explanations[5][16]. This search balances individual operation feature changes against 
global schedule impacts, bridging combinatorial optimization directly with post-hoc interpretability[5][17]. 
• Digital Twins as the Training Environment for DRL: Rather than acting merely as visual monitoring 
tools, Digital Twins serve as high-fidelity simulation environments for offline DRL policy training[12][18]. 
Once trained via Monte Carlo interactions inside the Digital Twin, the lightweight policy functions are 
deployed online to execute sub-second real-time adjustments on the physical shop floor [12]. 
• Service-Oriented Marketplaces for Off-Spec Product Recovery: The integration of Multi-Agent 
Systems (MAS) with Semantic Web Ontologies (SOA) enables real-time virtual auctions[20][21]. When a 
steel coil fails target quality metrics during hot rolling, product agents independently evaluate 
downstream transformation options (e.g., cold rolling, galvanizing) and bid in real-time order 
marketplaces to dynamically reallocate the product without stopping production

TASK 3 
An analysis of the literature reveals five primary methodological tensions and structural conflicts across 
furnace scheduling, energy optimization, and industrial automation. Below is an explicit contrast of these 
competing methodologies, followed by the strategic trade-offs your organization faces. 
 
Key Methodological Tensions & Contrasting Approaches 
1. Furnace Modeling: Static Mode Graphs vs. Continuous Bilinear Dynamic Control 
• Finite-State Machine / Mode Graph Approach: Traditional energy-aware scheduling models simplify 
machine behavior into a small set of discrete operational states (e.g., "processing" , "standby" , "off") 
governed by static state transition graphs with constant transition times and energy costs[1]. 
• Continuous Bilinear Optimal Control Approach: Advanced thermal models replace rigid discrete 
states with continuous bilinear differential equations that capture continuous heat loss and power 
dynamics[1]. By applying Pontryagin's Minimum Principle (PMP), these models derive a concave idle 
energy function that proves open-loop control (switching from zero power to maximum heating at an 
optimal time) achieves lower energy consumption than discrete mode switching[1]. 
• Core Contrast: Static mode models are easy to formulate within standard Integer Linear Programming 
(ILP) or genetic algorithms, but oversimplify furnace thermal dynamics and miss significant energy 
savings[1]. Continuous bilinear optimal control yields superior real-world energy reductions, but requires 
strict mathematical properties (such as concavity of the idle energy function) and precise parameter 
identification[1]. 
2. Optimization Paradigm: Deterministic MILP/MPC vs. Autonomous Deep Reinforcement Learning 
(DRL) 
• Mathematical Programming & MPC: Formulates scheduling problems using Mixed-Integer Linear 
Programming (MILP), Model Predictive Control (MPC), or exact Benders' decomposition[10]. These 
approaches aim for guaranteed global mathematical optimality or robust worst-case bounds[10]. 
• Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL / MARL): Models production scheduling as a Partially Observable 
Markov Decision Process (POMDP) or multi-agent game[10]. Algorithms such as Soft Actor-Critic (SAC), 
Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization (MAPPO), or attention-based DRL shift the heavy 
computational burden offline to train policy neural networks[10]. 
• Core Contrast: MILP and MPC provide exact optimality certificates under deterministic or nominal 
conditions, but suffer from severe online computational intractability and combinatorial explosion in 
large-scale multi-stage batch environments[12]. DRL and MARL deliver microsecond-level online 
decision-making to adaptively respond to volatile spot-market electricity prices and renewable 
generation[10], but lack mathematical optimality guarantees, depend heavily on reward function 
engineering, and risk converging to poor local optima without specialized attention mechanisms or 
heuristic action spaces[10]. 
3. Uncertainty Management: Fuzzy Logic vs. Stochastic Optimization vs. Robust Optimization 

• Fuzzy Logic Frameworks: Model vague or qualitative operational parameters (such as natural gas 
heating values, processing times, and due dates) using triangular fuzzy membership functions and 
generalized fuzzy dominance rules in metaheuristics like NSGA-II[23]. 
• Stochastic Optimization (SO): Assumes probability distributions of uncertain variables (e.g., job 
release times, electricity prices) and uses chance-constrained programming or Monte Carlo 
sampling[27]. 
• Robust Optimization (RO): Constructs bounded uncertainty sets and optimizes against the worst-case 
scenario without assuming underlying probability distributions[13]. 
• Two-Stage Hybrid DRL Frameworks: Combine offline distributed optimization (ALADIN) with online 
Fuzzy C-Means (FCM) clustering to dynamically adjust scheduling decisions between the boundaries of 
RO and SO[17]. 
• Core Contrast: Fuzzy logic is computationally fast when historical data is insufficient to construct 
probability distributions, but relies on subjective membership definitions[23]. Stochastic optimization 
performs well under known distributions, but exposes plants to severe operational failure when real-
world distributions shift[31][35]. Robust optimization guarantees feasibility under any scenario within the 
uncertainty set, but suffers from extreme conservatism, resulting in excessively high economic costs[31]. 
Data-driven hybrid DRL methods bridge the gap between RO conservatism and SO risk, but increase 
system complexity[17]. 
4. Automation Paradigm: Fully Autonomous AI vs. Human-Centric Intelligence Augmentation (IA) & XAI 
• Fully Automated AI (Industry 4.0): Relies on autonomous black-box neural networks or automated 
control loops to optimize throughput, makespan, and energy efficiency without human intervention [37]. 
• Intelligence Augmentation & Explainable AI (Industry 5.0 / TUPLES) : Integrates Explainable AI (XAI)—
such as counterfactual explanations, decision tree approximations of genetic algorithms, and SHAP 
feature-attribution maps—with human-in-the-loop (HiL) and human-on-the-loop (HoL) architectures[37]. 
Incorporates real-time operator state tracking (e.g., smartwatches for Dynamic Break Integration) and 
safety standards (ISA 84/IEC 61511)[42]. 
• Core Contrast: Full automation maximizes decision speed and raw optimization performance based 
strictly on system data, but fails to account for unmodeled social, financial, or safety context and risks 
catastrophic failure during out-of-distribution disruptions[37]. Human-centric IA and XAI ensure 
regulatory safety compliance, foster operator trust, and mitigate fatigue-induced errors[42], but introduce 
human interaction latency, potential AI-human decision conflicts, and lower theoretical peak 
automation throughput[54]. 
 
Mandatory Organizational Trade-Offs 
Based on these conflicting methodologies, your organization faces four critical strategic trade-offs: 
1. Modeling Accuracy vs. Computational Tractability in Furnace Operations: Adopting continuous 
bilinear optimal control for heating furnaces captures physical heat dissipation and maximizes energy 
savings, but requires solving complex nonlinear control equations[1]. Conversely, simplifying furnaces 
into static mode graphs simplifies mathematical integration into plant-wide solvers, but locks in higher 
baseline idle energy consumption[1]. 
2. Real-Time Adaptability vs. Guaranteed Global Optimality: Deploying DRL or MARL enables sub-
second real-time rescheduling in response to dynamic electricity spot prices and renewable energy 

fluctuations[10]. However, you must sacrifice the mathematical proof of global optimality and 
deterministic constraint bounds provided by offline MILP solvers[10]. 
3. Economic Efficiency vs. Operational Risk Under Uncertainty: Relying on Stochastic Optimization 
(SO) or nominal forecasts yields lower expected operational costs, but exposes the plant to severe 
disruptions if unexpected delays or price spikes occur[31][35]. Choosing Robust Optimization (RO) 
protects against worst-case disruptions, but forces the organization to accept significantly higher fuel 
and energy costs due to over-conservatism[31]. 
4. Throughput Maximization vs. Thermal Deterioration & Due Date Tardiness: Holding slabs at ambient 
temperature to batch similar steel grades reduces furnace setup times and gas consumption, but 
causes a severe slab deterioration effect[58]. Cold slabs require substantially longer furnace reheating 
times, which increases overall energy consumption and risks delaying downstream hot-rolling 
schedules[58]. 
5. Autonomous Efficiency vs. Industrial Process Safety & Operator Trust: Implementing fully 
autonomous DRL control loops eliminates labor dependencies and accelerates scheduling reactions, 
but risks operational safety violations during unexpected sensor or mechanical faults[37]. Transitioning to 
an Industry 5.0 Human-in-the-Loop architecture ensures ISA 84/IEC 61511 safety compliance and 
operator trust through XAI, but requires investment in operator interfaces (e.g., smartwatch DBI tracking) 
and accepts decision latency

1. Digital Twin (DT) Infrastructure (Physical-Virtual Mapping Layer) 
The Digital Twin serves as the centralized "data continent" connecting physical steelmaking plant assets 
with virtual optimization models[1]: 

• Standardized Asset Metamodels: Production assets across continuous casting, reheating furnaces, 
and rolling mills are represented using standardized Asset Administration Shells (AAS) or 5D virtual 
models[1]. 
• Real-Time IIoT Ingestion: The virtual environment continuously synchronizes multi-source telemetry 
from Manufacturing Execution Systems (MES) and Distributed Control Systems (DCS), tracking live slab 
positions, furnace zone temperatures, by-product gas holder levels, and grid spot-market tariffs[6]. 
• Physics & Logistics Constraints: The DT enforces physical operational mechanics—such as First-In-
First-Out (FIFO) slab movement through walking beam furnaces, crane handling intervals, holding pit 
limits, and mechanical interlocks between charging, stepping, and extracting operations[10]. 
2. Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) Engine (Real-Time Execution Layer) 
The DRL layer replaces computationally intensive offline mathematical programs (e.g., high-dimensional 
MILP) with microsecond online policy evaluations[13]: 
• POMDP & MARL Formulation: Production scheduling is modeled as a Partially Observable Markov 
Decision Process (POMDP) or Multi-Agent System (MARL), assigning independent agents to discrete 
equipment nodes (e.g., Electric Arc Furnaces, walking beam furnaces, continuous casters)[13]. 
• Closed-Loop Offline-to-Online Control: Agent policy neural networks are trained offline within the 
Digital Twin environment using Soft Actor-Critic (SAC), Evolutionary Search with attention mechanisms, 
or ALADIN distributed optimization[6]. Once trained, the policy network evaluates live state observations 
in milliseconds to execute real-time control actions[7]. 
• Adaptive Multi-Tiered Rescheduling: When real-world disruptions occur (such as machine 
breakdowns or molten iron release delays), the system adaptively selects an appropriate dynamic 
response—ranging from flexible time fine-tuning for minor delays, to local machine exchange, up to 
global rescheduling[20][21]. 
3. Explainable AI (XAI) & Human Governance (Trust & Safety Layer) 
XAI deconstructs complex deep learning models into transparent, human-understandable rationales to 
ensure operational safety and operator trust[17]: 
• Post-Hoc Feature Attribution & Symbolic Models: Interpretability techniques—including SHAP values, 
LIME, decision tree approximations, and symbolic Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KAN)—deconstruct 
neural network policy decisions into feature-influence force plots[25]. Operators can verify how 
parameters like real-time electricity prices, raw material availability, or shift staffing drove a specific 
scheduling action[26][30]. 
• Multi-Objective Counterfactual Search: Counterfactual explanation engines evaluate alternative 
schedule modifications, showing managers the precise operational feature adjustments needed to 
achieve a target makespan or energy reduction[31]. 
• Human-in-the-Loop (HiL) & Process Safety: Complying with Industry 5.0 principles and ISA 84/IEC 
61511 safety standards, human operators retain override authority for critical actions. Real-time 
operator monitoring (e.g., smartwatch Dynamic Break Integration) balances automated plant 
performance with worker well-being and fatigue limits[23][32].

Executive Briefing: The DRL-DT-XAI Blueprint for Autonomous Steelmaking Optimization 
1. Introduction: Strategic Imperative for Intelligent Production 
In the hyper-competitive global steel market, the shift toward autonomous production is no longer a 
visionary goal but a survival necessity. Traditional scheduling models are fundamentally static, failing to 
account for the complex time-domain dynamics of high-heat environments. This failure results in massive 
margin erosion as systems struggle to manage the "stochastic" volatility of machine breakdowns and 
energy-intensive idle periods. 
The integration of Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL), Digital Twins (DT), and Explainable AI (XAI) offers a 
unified architecture to transform these operational liabilities into proactive advantages. By modeling the 
thermal physics of the furnace and the probability of equipment failure, we can move from reactive 
firefighting to optimized, real-time control. 
Strategic Value Proposition The DRL-DT-XAI framework replaces antiquated "static mode" scheduling with 
a high-fidelity autonomous intelligence. By leveraging bilinear Digital Twins and proactive DRL policies, this 
blueprint eliminates wasteful idle energy consumption and mitigates the "preempt-repeat" costs of machine 
failure, directly securing margins against the compounding effects of heat loss and production disruptions. 
As energy volatility and operational stability become the primary differentiators of plant profitability, the 
industry must move beyond the status quo to address the underlying drivers of cost. 
 
2. ATTENTION: The Urgency of Energy Inefficiency and Operational Volatility 
Steel-hardening furnaces are the primary cost drivers in modern plants, yet they are often managed with 
remarkably coarse logic. Maintaining a furnace at an operating temperature of 960°C requires a continuous 
power input of approximately 40kW. In a "static" scheduling environment, this energy is wasted during every 
idle period between tasks. 
Furthermore, the industry suffers from the "deterioration effect"—a mathematical reality where the actual 
processing time of a steel ingot is a non-decreasing function of its waiting time. The longer an ingot waits due 
to poor scheduling or machine breakdown, the more heat it loses, requiring expensive reheating and 
extended soaking durations. Under "preempt-repeat" conditions, a single machine breakdown can force an 
entire batch to be re-processed from scratch, multiplying energy and resource costs. 
Critical Vulnerabilities in Status Quo Operations 
• Restrictive Finite State Models: Current "On/Off/Standby" logic is too coarse to capture the nuanced 
thermal curves of industrial furnaces, missing optimized cooling/heating windows. 
• Stochastic Breakdown Fragility: Without proactive sequence modeling, unexpected machine failures 
cause massive start-time deviations that the system cannot absorb. 
• Cumulative Deterioration Costs: Inefficient scheduling causes ingots to wait longer, leading to 
increased rolling times and higher fuel consumption to restore required temperatures. 
 
3. INTEREST: Digital Twins and DRL—The Engine of Feasibility 

The engine of this blueprint is the transition from simplified linear models to high-fidelity "bilinear system" 
approximations. This Digital Twin (DT) approach maps the time-domain dynamics of the furnace using 
specific parameters ($a, b, q$) that account for thermal resistance and power input impacts. 
This high-fidelity modeling is the prerequisite for Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) success. While 
traditional scheduling is an NP-hard challenge, our approach reduces complexity to $O(n^3)$—a 
polynomial-time efficiency that enables the DRL controller to make instant, real-time rescheduling 
decisions in response to disruptions.

4. DESIRE: Safety, Governance, and Trust via XAI Transparency 
In high-stakes manufacturing, "black box" AI is a liability that risks catastrophic scheduling errors during 
maintenance windows. Stakeholder trust is only possible through a transparent "Governance Layer" 
provided by Explainable AI (XAI). 
This framework utilizes XAI to perform "Job Attribute Prioritization. " Instead of obscure heuristics, the system 
calculates a job's flexibility measure ($F_j$), which is a composite of its processing time ($p_j$), available 
compressibility ($w_j$), and the average slope of its resource cost function ($D_j$). Operators can clearly 
see why certain ingots are prioritized based on their ability to absorb downtime without triggering "preempt-
repeat" costs. 
The Governance Layer: XAI Differentiators 
• Transparency: Moves beyond hidden logic to clear attribute prioritization, allowing humans to audit how 
the system handles $F_j$ measures. 
• Trust via Surrogates: We use Support Vector Regression (SVR) to solve the "computational burden" of 
simulating thousands of breakdown scenarios. XAI explains these SVR approximations, allowing 
operators to validate the AI’s robustness logic. 
• Safety: Explainable logic identifies which jobs have the most "cushion" to survive a machine failure, 
preventing sequences that would lead to total batch loss. 
 

5. ACTION: Phased Deployment Roadmap 
To ensure production continuity, we will prioritize a structured, three-phase rollout that integrates thermal 
physics with proactive scheduling. 
1. Phase I: System Identification & DT Calibration: We will derive the bilinear model parameters ($a, b, 
q$) from existing furnace telemetry to create a high-fidelity Digital Twin of the heating and cooling 
cycles. 
2. Phase II: DRL Training & Proactive Buffering: We will deploy the SVR-assisted NSGA-II optimization 
engine to train our DRL agent. This agent will learn to proactively sequence jobs to balance robustness 
(mean rescheduling cost) and stability (variance) against stochastic machine breakdowns. 
3. Phase III: XAI Integration & Full Autonomy: We will implement the job attribute prioritization 
procedure, providing operators with XAI-driven insights into ingot flexibility. Once trust is established, 
the system will shift to full autonomous control. 
Executive Call to Action The DRL-DT-XAI blueprint is the only methodology capable of achieving $O(n^3)$ 
computational efficiency for instant rescheduling while simultaneously minimizing idle energy waste. By 
moving to this proactive, explainable framework, we will eliminate the "wasteful" paradigms of the past, 
mitigate the deterioration effect, and secure the plant’s competitive advantage through autonomous 
precision.
